item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating history dependence, recency, and order sensitivity. [Does It Look Sequential? (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) uses sequence shuffling across 15 datasets and finds several popular benchmarks have weak sequential structure. [Disentangling User and Item Sequence Patterns (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) compares random shuffling with shuffling constrained by item availability; apparent sequential signal can arise from user behavior, item availability, or both. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduces a dedicated recency metric, reporting that excessive recent-item emphasis can accompany poorer recommendation performance.\n\nA [2026 temporal-attribution preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27201) explicitly examines popularity confounding and input corruption, highlighting the need to assess attribution faithfulness rather than interpret raw attention as importance. Its separately trained masking probe falls outside this task’s single-model constraint. A compatible diagnostic proposal is to freeze the trained GRU4Rec and evaluate existing training-prefix/next-target pairs under intact history, oldest-prefix deletion, equal-sized recent-history deletion, random deletion, and history shuffling that preserves the last item. Keep each target and candidate set fixed; retain left padding and final-nonpadding readout. Compare paired changes in target rank, HR@10, and target-versus-negative margins; use user-clustered bootstrap intervals and strata defined by training-only target popularity and history length. These controls help distinguish older-context dependence from deletion size and order sensitivity, but cannot fully eliminate positional or distribution-shift effects. Interpret results as model sensitivity, not evidence that older interactions represent stale intent. This protocol is a synthesis of the literature, rather than a verified standard matched-target intervention method."}
